abstract.text: Ten EMS agencies serving 1.5 million people across nine U.S. states contributed data to the AHUP-CPR Registry. A total of 3,709 OHCA patients met enrollment criteria. Across five years, (2020-2024), the average (± SD) interval from 9-1-1 call receipt-to-professional CPR was 9.62 ± 5.78 min. Incidence of ROSC, HD, and HD-FN were 29.5%, 13.1%, and 10.5%, respectively. The incidence of HD-FN for patients presenting with a shockable rhythm meeting Utstein criteria, pulseless electrical activity, or asystole were 33.9%, 11.8%, and 2.0%, respectively. Among 391 neurologically favorable survivors, 91% had a Cerebral Performance Category score of 1 (normal or near normal brain function) at HD. The average age of the survivors was 56.8 ± 16.3 years. Age, interval from 9-1-1 call to professional CPR, witnessed status, and initial rhythm were the most significant predictors of HD-FN using multivariable Poisson regression.

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: In this 5-year observational registry study, use of AHUP-CPR for the treatment of OHCA was associated with survival to HD of 13.1% and HD-FN of 10.5% in the overall cohort, which comprised patients presenting in shockable rhythms, PEA, and asystole. Drawn from 3,709 OHCA patients treated across diverse EMS systems, these findings provide the largest clinical practice-based characterization to date of the outcomes associated with early transition to AHUP-CPR.

articles.title: Prehospital Resource Utilization After Video-Assisted Versus Telephone-Only Emergency Calls: A Post Hoc Analysis of the CAM-VISION Cluster Randomized Clinical Trial.

abstract.label: OBJECTIVES
abstract.text: To examine whether video assistance during emergency calls reduced actual prehospital resource utilization across the complete response pathway compared with telephone-only calls.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: This post hoc analysis included 18,745 calls from the cluster-randomized CAM-VISION parent trial (NCT05742412; 8,124 video; 10,621 telephone only). Outcomes were assessed at call level according to telecommunicator allocation and included unit dispatch, pathway progression, number of units, and cumulative unit time. Effects were estimated with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) accounting for clustering by telecommunicator.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Initial unit dispatch occurred in 69.4% of video-group calls and 73.9% of telephone-only calls (risk difference, -4.5 percentage points; 95% confidence intervals (CI) (-10.0 to 1.0). Among calls with no unit initially dispatched, subsequent unit dispatch was uncommon (5.1% vs 5.5%). Across the complete response pathway, 71.0% versus 75.3% received at least 1 unit (risk difference, -4.4 percentage points; 95% CI, -9.6 to 0.8), and 69.3% versus 73.8% had a unit reach the scene (risk difference, -4.5 percentage points; 95% CI, -10.0 to 1.0). More than 1 unit was dispatched in 23.3% versus 25.0%. Mean units per call were 1.005 versus 1.054 (mean difference, -0.049; 95% CI, -0.148 to 0.049); mean cumulative unit time was 52.8 versus 54.3 minutes (mean difference, -1.5; 95% CI, -6.2 to 3.1). Overall, differences in initial dispatch were concentrated in ambulance use.

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: No statistically significant absolute differences in conventional prehospital resource utilization were observed. Point estimates were consistently lower in the video group, primarily through fewer initial dispatches, and subsequent dispatch did not materially offset this numerical difference.

articles.title: Spatiotemporal dynamics of human metapneumovirus and potential impact of respiratory syncytial virus interventions in the United States.

abstract.text: Human metapneumovirus (HMPV) causes acute lower respiratory infections, primarily affecting young children and older adults, with seasonal outbreaks peaking annually in March or April in the United States and other temperate regions in the Northern hemisphere. However, the factors driving HMPV seasonality in the United States remain poorly understood. We analyzed laboratory-confirmed HMPV cases and age-specific emergency department visits across 10 US regions, fitting an age-stratified dynamic transmission model to assess spatiotemporal patterns and investigate the influence of environmental variables and viral interference from RSV on HMPV transmission rates. We found that models incorporating climate variables into the transmission rate, including vapor pressure, precipitation, potential evapotranspiration, and minimum temperature, could not capture the timing of HMPV activity across all regions. Instead, HMPV timing was associated with RSV activity, with the HMPV transmission rate reduced in the presence of RSV. We showed that among the candidate models considered, only the models that included an RSV-associated term could reproduce the biennial pattern of HMPV observed in some regions, characterized by alternating "late-small" and "early-large" epidemics. When the best-fit model including the RSV-associated term was used to predict the potential impact of RSV interventions on HMPV transmission, we found that RSV interventions are unlikely to result in a substantial increase in HMPV activity despite reducing competition from RSV. Our work unravels the spatiotemporal dynamics of HMPV and its interaction with RSV, informing future seasonal forecasting and intervention strategies for HMPV.

articles.title: Age as a determinant of trampoline-related oral-facial-head injuries in pediatric emergency department visits: A NEISS analysis.

abstract.text: Over the last decade trampoline use has increased. Many injuries occur that require emergency department (ED) care. The purpose of this research is to examine the role of age in trampoline-related oral-facial-head injuries that require ED care. Data from the 2024 National Electronic Injury Surveillance System (NEISS) was used. Trampoline-related injuries were extracted from the data set. Oral-facial-head trampoline-related injuries were compared with other types of trampoline-related injuries by age groups (0 to <6 years, 6 to <12 years, and 12 to ≤18 years) in Chi-Square analyses and logistic regression analyses. There were 3548 NEISS-reported trampoline-associated injuries for children, ages 0 to ≤18 years, in 2024. This corresponded to an estimated 101,474 trampoline injuries in the United States in 2024. Of these, 21.7% were oral-facial-head trampoline-related injuries (weighted estimate of 22,033 injuries). Of all the trampoline-related injuries in children ages 0 to ≤18 years, children ages 0 to <6 years had 33.0% of the injuries; children ages 6 to <12 years had 51.9%; and, children ages 12 to ≤18 years had 15.1%. Children ages 0 to <6 years had an adjusted odds ratio of 1.66 [95% CI: 1.11, 2.50; p = 0.0155] compared with children ages 12 to ≤18 years for oral-facial-head trampoline-related injuries as compared with other injuries from trampolines. Younger children have significantly higher odds of trampoline-related oral-facial-head injuries requiring emergency department care compared with adolescents, supporting age as an important host factor within the Haddon Matrix framework. These findings highlight the need for targeted prevention and anticipatory guidance for younger children.

articles.title: A National Poison Data System® description of neonatal opioid withdrawal syndrome related to maternal kratom use.

abstract.label: INTRODUCTION
abstract.text: Kratom is a drug derived from the Mitragyna speciosa tree that can exhibit dose-dependent stimulant, analgesic, and sedative effects through mu-opioid agonism and other mechanisms. In the United States, kratom is regulated at the state and local level in some areas but is not federally regulated. As such, it is available for purchase at head shops and gas stations in many markets, as well as through the internet. There are limited data describing Neonatal Opioid Withdrawal Syndrome in children born to mothers using kratom. We seek to further describe neonatal kratom-associated withdrawal using cases reported to United States poison centers.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: This was a retrospective observational study using the National Poison Data System®. We queried the National Poison Data System® for all exposures of kratom in children < 21 days of age from January 1, 2015 through December 31, 2023. We reviewed de-identified notes, or poison centers completed an online data entry form to provide additional data about the exposure.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: There were 20 reported exposures; 14 were included. Median symptom duration was eight days. Symptoms included agitation, tremor, increased tone, tachypnea, decrease oral intake, and weight loss. Nine of 14 received opioid therapy (most commonly morphine and/or methadone), generally starting within 1-3 days after the consult when reported.

abstract.label: DISCUSSION
abstract.text: Neonatal opioid withdrawal syndrome may occur in a child exposed to kratom in utero. Our data predate widespread availability of 7-hydroxymitragynine products and exposures were reported only as kratom, limiting the interpretation about current risks.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: Maternal use of kratom during pregnancy is associated with neonatal opioid withdrawal syndrome in neonates immediately or shortly following birth. Women who are pregnant or are planning to become pregnant and use kratom should be counseled on possible risks.

articles.title: Suzetrigine as a novel treatment for refractory neuropathic pain in ciguatera poisoning.
Pediatric forensic cases during the COVID 19 lockdown and reopening periods: a retrospective cohort study from a tertiary care pediatric emergency department.

abstract.text: The COVID‑19 lockdown disrupted daily life, altering children's exposure to risks and reshaping emergency department utilisation. Understanding how these changes influenced pediatric forensic epidemiology is essential for prevention and policy development. All forensic cases involving children aged 1 month-18 years were included. Two periods were analysed: the COVID-19 lockdown period (March 2020-June 2021) and the post-lockdown period (June 2021-March 2024). Data on demographics, causes, outcomes and costs were extracted from medical and forensic records. During the COVID‑19 lockdown period, the incidence of forensic cases was 25.8 per 1000 PED visits per month, whereas during the reopening period this rate decreased to 12.7 per 1000 PED visits per month (p < 0.001). Exposure to chemical substances and assault were more frequent during the lockdown period (p = 0.01 and p = 0.001, respectively), whereas food poisoning was more common during the reopening period (p = 0.004). Forensic cases were predominant among female adolescents (p = 0.004). Male sex was associated with a significantly higher likelihood of forensic cases (OR = 1.25, 95% CI: 1.05-1.49, p = 0.011). Furthermore, the COVID-19 lockdown period was independently associated with an increased odds of forensic cases (OR = 2.06, 95% CI: 1.65-2.56, p < 0.001). The median outpatient and total bills per PED visit were lower in forensic cases (48.7 vs. 68.1 TRY, p < 0.001 and 57.8 vs. 90.2 TRY, p < 0.001, respectively). Different COVID‑19 periods were associated with significant differences in the incidence, causes, and patterns of pediatric forensic cases. Male sex and the lockdown period were identified as independent risk factors for forensic presentations, highlighting the complex interaction between demographic and temporal factors in forensic epidemiology.

articles.title: Stroke unit capacity and acute stroke care systems in Sub-Saharan Africa: progress, gaps, and implementation challenges.
articles.journal_full: Neurological sciences : official journal of the Italian Neurological Society and of the Italian Society of Clinical Neurophysiology

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Stroke is a leading cause of death and disability across sub-Saharan Africa (SSA), yet the infrastructure required for effective acute management remains severely limited across much of the region.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: This narrative review critically appraises the available evidence on stroke unit availability and acute stroke care capacity in sub-Saharan Africa, including data on reperfusion therapies, neuroimaging infrastructure, workforce capacity, and implementation studies from diverse SSA settings.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: The literature reviewed demonstrates major deficits in dedicated stroke units, reperfusion therapies, neuroimaging infrastructure, and trained stroke specialists. Only a minority of SSA hospitals have functional stroke units, and intravenous thrombolysis rates remain extremely low in most settings. However, implementation studies from Guinea, South Africa, and Kenya demonstrate that organized stroke care is feasible and can improve outcomes even under substantial resource constraints. These findings challenge the assumption that evidence-based stroke care is inherently unsuitable for SSA health systems; rather, they point to failures in policy prioritization and structural underinvestment as the primary drivers of current deficits. Hemorrhagic stroke management, particularly structured intracerebral hemorrhage care bundles, represents a distinct and largely unaddressed gap in the SSA literature. The methodological limitations of the available evidence base are critically appraised throughout.

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: Coordinated investment in stroke infrastructure, workforce development, prehospital systems, and context-specific implementation strategies is urgently needed to address the growing stroke burden across sub-Saharan Africa.

articles.title: Microbiota-gut-brain axis dysregulation in irritable bowel syndrome: mechanisms, clinical evidence, and therapeutic implications. a narrative review.

abstract.text: Irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) is a heterogeneous disorder of gut-brain interaction in which altered visceral sensitivity, motility, immune activity, epithelial permeability, and microbial metabolism may interact. Microbiota-related associations are frequently reported, but their direction and causal relevance remain uncertain. This narrative review critically examines clinical and mechanistic evidence concerning microbiota-gut-brain communication in IBS, including short-chain fatty acids, bile acids, gaseous metabolites, tryptophan metabolism, environmental exposures, and microbiota-directed interventions. The literature was selected for relevance and interpretability rather than through a systematic evidence-synthesis protocol. Across studies, microbiota-associated differences vary by phenotype, diet, geography, sampling site, and analytical method; no validated IBS-specific microbial signature has emerged. Bile acid metabolism, mucosal immune-neural interactions, and microbial metabolites provide plausible mechanistic links, although much evidence remains associative. Low-FODMAP dietary treatment and rifaximin in appropriately selected patients have clinical trial support, whereas probiotic effects are formulation dependent and fecal microbiota transplantation remains investigational. Microbiome-based precision treatment requires longitudinal phenotyping, standardized sampling, functional multi-omics, and intervention studies demonstrating that microbial or metabolic changes mediate clinical benefit. Microbiome profiling is not yet established as a routine diagnostic test for IBS.

articles.title: Association of Walch glenoid morphology and fracture patterns in proximal humeral fractures.
articles.journal_full: European journal of trauma and emergency surgery : official publication of the European Trauma Society

abstract.label: PURPOSE
abstract.text: Proximal humeral fracture (PHF) assessment focuses on fracture pattern, bone quality, and patient factors, whereas glenoid morphology-central to biomechanics in glenohumeral arthritis and instability-is overlooked. We hypothesized that glenoid morphology consistent with Walch type B (posterior decentring) is independently associated with complex, tuberculum-involving PHFs.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: This single-centre, retrospective cohort study analysed 919 patients with a PHF and shoulder computed tomography (CT). Two blinded shoulder-subspecialized orthopedic trauma surgeons independently classified all cases; agreement was quantified with Cohen's κ. Fractures were classified by the Neer and AO/OTA systems and glenoid morphology by the Walch classification. The primary outcome-tuberculum involvement (Neer IV/V)-was analysed by multivariable logistic regression adjusted for age at trauma, sex, and osteoarthritis.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: The cohort comprised 919 patients (72.6% female; median age at trauma 69 years). The Walch distribution in this CT-selected cohort was type A 42.7%, B 54.4%, C 2.7%, and D 0.2%; osteoarthritis was present in 59.5%. Walch agreement was moderate (κ = 0.53), with disagreement concentrated at the A1↔B1 decentring boundary (p < 0.001). Walch type B was independently associated with tuberculum involvement (adjusted OR 2.07, 95% CI 1.56-2.74; adjusted RR 1.30, 95% CI 1.17-1.45; both p < 0.001) and with greater AO/OTA fracture complexity (adjusted ordinal OR 1.60, p < 0.001). Female sex was independently associated with the outcome (adjusted OR 1.44, 95% CI 1.05-1.97, p = 0.023); age and osteoarthritis were not significant.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: In this CT-selected study population, glenoid morphology consistent with Walch type B was independently associated with complex, tuberculum-involving proximal humeral fractures. The association was statistically robust but clinically modest (AUC 0.62), and Walch type B morphology represented one of several correlates of fracture pattern rather than a standalone predictor. Glenoid morphology may therefore be worth recording during CT and fracture-pattern assessment; these hypothesis-generating findings are not sufficient to modify current treatment algorithms, but support the inclusion of glenoid parameters in future risk models and prospective studies.

abstract.label: LEVEL OF EVIDENCE
abstract.text: Level III retrospective cohort study prognostic study.

articles.title: Real-World Outcomes After Dupilumab Initiation for Pediatric Chronic Rhinosinusitis with Nasal Polyps.
articles.journal_full: Otolaryngology--head and neck surgery : official journal of American Academy of Otolaryngology-Head and Neck Surgery

abstract.label: OBJECTIVE
abstract.text: To evaluate whether dupilumab initiation is associated with reduced short-term flare burden, healthcare utilization, and surgical escalation in pediatric patients with chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyps (CRSwNP).

abstract.label: STUDY DESIGN
abstract.text: Retrospective cohort study.

abstract.label: SETTING
abstract.text: TriNetX United States Collaborative Network.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: Patients aged ≤18 years with chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyps were identified between January 1, 2015, and December 31, 2024. Dupilumab-treated patients were indexed at treatment initiation and propensity score-matched 1:1 to nondupilumab controls indexed at a systemic corticosteroid burst based on asthma, atopic dermatitis, allergic rhinitis, and prior endoscopic sinus surgery. Outcomes within 12 months were compared using risk ratios.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: In 442 matched patients (221 per cohort), dupilumab-treated patients had lower rates of acute sinusitis (12/221 [5.4%] vs 31/221 [14.0%]; risk ratio [RR] 0.39; 95% CI: 0.20-0.73; P = .002), systemic corticosteroid bursts (80/221 [36.2%] vs 101/221 [45.7%]; RR 0.79; 95% CI: 0.63-0.99; P = .042), and functional endoscopic sinus surgery (19/221 [8.6%] vs 38/221 [17.2%]; RR 0.50; 95% CI: 0.30-0.84; P = .007). Nasal polyp diagnoses were more frequently documented in the dupilumab-treated cohort (148/221 [67.0%] vs 95/221 [43.0%]; P < .0001), while emergency department visits (16/221 [7.2%] vs 27/221 [12.2%]; P = .078) and inpatient admissions (12/221 [5.4%] vs 16/221 [7.2%]; P = .435) were similar between cohorts.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: These findings suggest that dupilumab may be a steroid-sparing and surgery-sparing option in pediatric CRSwNP.

articles.title: What makes a bridge program a bridge program? Toward evidence-based standards for emergency department-initiated opioid use disorder treatment.

abstract.label: BACKGROUND AND OBJECTIVES
abstract.text: Emergency department (ED)-based bridge programs for opioid use disorder (OUD) have proliferated in response to the opioid overdose crisis. Despite a consistent evidence base, variation exists in program design and implementation in real-world hospital settings, and "bridge program" has become a catch-all term for interventions linking patients to OUD treatment. This narrative review proposes evidence-based standards.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: PubMed, PsycINFO, and Google Scholar were searched for articles, consensus statements, and implementation reports published through May 2026. Reference lists and systematic reviews were reviewed. A narrative synthesis identified essential programmatic elements and distinguished the ED-based bridge program from related approaches.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Six essential elements were identified: (1) same-day medication initiation; (2) bedside dispensing of a short-term medication supply before discharge; (3) 24/7 operational coverage; (4) designated on-site workspace for program personnel; (5) facilitated linkage to ongoing outpatient care via warm handoff; and (6) naloxone distribution at every ED encounter.

abstract.label: DISCUSSION AND CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: Programs self-identifying as bridge programs without these elements may still provide value but are not delivering care in alignment with the evidence base, and their outcomes may reflect that gap. The framework offered here is intended as a best practice resource for organizations working within real-world constraints.

abstract.label: SCIENTIFIC SIGNIFICANCE
abstract.text: Establishing common terminology, delineating ED bridge programs from standalone peer navigator or referral programs, and documenting the evidence underlying each element provides a practical roadmap for assessing fidelity and improvement. This framework can inform standards of care and investment decisions by funders, administrators, and policymakers.

articles.title: Impact of 22 Comorbidities on Number of Hospitalizations and Emergency Department Visits in U.S. Community-Dwelling Older Adults With Alzheimer's Disease and Related Dementias (AD/ADRD).
articles.journal_full: Journal of applied gerontology : the official journal of the Southern Gerontological Society

abstract.text: ObjectivesExamine the impact of 22 comorbidities on number of hospitalizations and Emergency Department (ED) visits among community-dwelling persons with Alzheimer's Disease and Alzheimer's Disease Related Dementias (AD/ADRD).MethodsAnalyzed 2018-2019 Medicare Claims data for 7.1 million beneficiaries aged ≥65 with AD/ADRD. Each comorbidity's impact was assessed using net effect (NE), a measure of attributable risk for multiple interacting factors.ResultsPneumonia showed the highest contribution to all-cause hospitalizations (NE = 1.58), indicating that pneumonia contributed 1.58 all-cause hospitalizations per year. Acute myocardial infarction had an NE of 1.37; hip fracture, 1.20; anemia, 0.89; and stroke, 0.78. Stroke had the highest contribution to all-cause ED visits (NE = 0.477), followed by arthritis (0.421), pneumonia (0.400), depression (0.394), hypertension (0.325), and hip fracture (0.323).ConclusionOur results highlight a large discrepancy in how the various comorbidities of AD/ADRD impact healthcare utilizations. Certain conditions, particularly pneumonia and arthritis, may be key targets for reducing hospitalizations and ED visits.

articles.title: Chemical Ordering of High-Entropy Nanomaterials for Pathway-Directed Electrocatalysis.

abstract.text: High-entropy nanomaterials (HEMs) have emerged as versatile electrocatalytic platforms, because their multielement compositions provide diverse electronic configurations and coordination environments. However, high configurational complexity alone does not define the catalytic sites. Differences in elemental interactions and reduction kinetics can lead to segregation, phase separation, and structural heterogeneity, while random site occupation complicates the identification of catalytic sites and structure-activity correlations. High-entropy chemical ordering (HECO) addresses this challenge by organizing selected elements over defined spatial scales while retaining the multielement diversity. Drawing on our studies and related works, this Account describes three connected strategies. Electrospinning-enabled coordination confinement uses metal-polymer coordination and a polymer-derived carbon matrix to establish homogeneous multielement phases and regulate atomic transport. Directional atomic migration organizes selected elements at surfaces and interfaces through segregation, exsolution, and migration trapping. Diffusion-mediated bulk ordering produces preferential occupation of crystallographic sublattices and long-range ordered high-entropy intermetallics (HEIs). Local electronic polarization and intermediate adsorption help determine the elementary steps favored at different sites, while structural evolution under operating conditions can modify these relationships. Spatial organization can influence the intermediate transfer, reaction selectivity, and competing pathways. These considerations can guide the design of new surface-, interfacial-, and bulk-ordered HEMs with catalytic functions tailored to pathway-directed electrocatalysis.

articles.title: Transmural and Intraluminal Gallbladder Hemorrhage (Hemocholecyst) in a Dog Following Snakebite Envenomation.
articles.journal: J Vet Emerg Crit Care (San Antonio)
articles.journal_full: Journal of veterinary emergency and critical care (San Antonio, Tex. : 2001)

abstract.label: OBJECTIVE
abstract.text: To describe a case of hemocholecyst as a sequela to snake envenomation in a dog.

abstract.label: CASE SUMMARY
abstract.text: A 2-year-old neutered male mixed-breed dog was hospitalized for 4 days after a suspected crotaline envenomation and possible anaphylactic reaction. Significant clinical findings included coagulopathy, thrombocytopenia, hyperbilirubinemia, anemia, multiorgan dysfunction, and hypotension. Point-of-care ultrasound was suggestive of gallbladder wall thickening, a finding frequently associated with anaphylaxis or intramural hemorrhage, with other differentials including cholecystitis, mucocele, or neoplasia. Despite aggressive therapy with antivenom, blood products, and supportive care, the dog experienced cardiopulmonary arrest. Necropsy revealed widespread hemorrhage, multiorgan tissue necrosis, pigment nephropathy, and marked obstructive hemorrhage and necrosis of the gallbladder, consistent with hemocholecyst formation.

abstract.label: NEW OR UNIQUE INFORMATION PROVIDED
abstract.text: To the authors' knowledge, this is the first report of hemocholecyst as a sequela to snake envenomation in a dog. Obstructive hemocholecyst and transmural gallbladder wall hemorrhage should remain differentials for severe hyperbilirubinemia in dogs with venom-induced coagulopathy.

articles.title: Preoperative Telehealth Versus In-Person Appointments Prior to Lumbar Fusion: Influence on Surgical Planning and Postoperative Outcomes.

abstract.label: STUDY DESIGN
abstract.text: Retrospective study.

abstract.label: OBJECTIVE
abstract.text: The purpose of this study is to evaluate the impact of attending a preoperative telehealth appointment, compared to in-person, on intraoperative surgical plan change and postoperative outcomes following lumbar fusion.

abstract.label: SUMMARY OF BACKGROUND DATA
abstract.text: Telehealth utilization for orthopedic appointments has greatly increased due to the COVID-19 pandemic. Spine surgery remains controversial, as surgical planning relies heavily on objective physical exam and imaging data. As such, controversy surrounding the utility and safety of telehealth in preoperative spine surgery planning remains.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: Adult patients who underwent elective lumbar fusion (2020-2022) were identified at a single tertiary center. Patients with a surgical indication of revision, malignancy, trauma, or infection were excluded. The final preoperative appointment type (telehealth vs. in-person) was determined. Surgical and clinical outcomes, including intraoperative surgical plan change, postoperative phone calls, in-person office visits, emergency department (ED) visits, opioid usage, and patient-reported outcome measures (PROMs), were collected. An α was set at 0.05.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Of 544 patients were included (18.8% telehealth). Utilization of telehealth appointments was similar before versus after COVID-19 restrictions were lifted in October 2021. Changes from preoperative surgical plan occurred at a similar rate between groups. Preoperative telehealth appointment was found to be an independent predictor of requiring fewer postoperative office visits (estimate: -0.55, P=0.002), but a higher likelihood of visiting the ED (OR: 4.59, P=0.011). Although telehealth users had decreased opioid utilization from 90 to 365 days postoperatively and improved VAS Back scores at 1 year after surgery, these findings were not significant on multivariable analysis.

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: Telehealth utilization in spine surgery remains common postpandemic. The current work showed that lumbar fusion preoperative planning via telehealth is reliable compared to in-person appointments. Interestingly, telehealth decreased postoperative office-visit utilization but increased ED visits. Further study is needed to investigate the clinical significance of these observations.

articles.title: High-fidelity simulation in preregistration nurse education: a framework for major incident preparedness.
articles.journal_full: Emergency nurse : the journal of the RCN Accident and Emergency Nursing Association

abstract.text: Increasing global risks mandate that all nurses possess major incident preparedness, however preregistration education in this area in the UK is inconsistent and frequently passive. Since 2022, the University of Derby, England, has provided high-fidelity, campus-based major incident simulations in which more than 300 nursing students from all fields have participated as active, autonomous professionals. Guided by a structured framework and evaluated against defined operational outputs, the student participants establish temporary receiving centres and manage complex, resource-constrained crisis scenarios. This article describes the design, structure and delivery of the major incident simulations and reports the findings of a rapid thematic analysis of student, academic facilitator and simulated patient post-simulation evaluation feedback. The findings indicate that active immersion in structured, high-fidelity major incident simulations can enhance students' self-awareness and reflection on their individual learning needs, consolidate their theoretical and clinical knowledge and identify their preparedness for major incident response.

articles.title: Dexmedetomidine Versus Propofol Induction for Sedated Radiologic Procedures in Patients With Trisomy 21.

abstract.label: OBJECTIVES
abstract.text: Patients with Trisomy 21 (T21) are more susceptible to sedation-related adverse events (AEs). Few studies address the risk of propofol or compare natural airway sedation regimens in this population. Dexmedetomidine (DEX) is less likely than propofol to result in AEs as it promotes a more natural sleep and less airway muscle relaxation.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: This study is a secondary analysis of prospectively collected data. We queried the Pediatric Sedation Research Consortium (PSRC) Database from the years 2020 to 2025. The demographic characteristics were summarized using descriptive statistics. The incidence of sedation-related AEs and sedation failures were described by induction drug (DEX vs. propofol). Any medication used other than DEX or propofol were excluded. We performed a propensity score analysis comparing the DEX cohort to the propofol cohort. All the statistical work was performed using SAS 9.4.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: A total of 337 patients met inclusion criteria. The average age was 7 years. Forty-four percent of AEs were partial airway obstruction. For the bivariate analyses, the AE outcome variable is statistically significant with the medication variable (χ2df=1=33.249, P<0.001). Induction with propofol had a 5 times higher odds of an AE (OR=5.069, 95% CI: 2.829-9.082). After propensity score matching, there are a total of 216 matched observations.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: In patients with T21 undergoing radiologic procedures, the odds of having any AE are higher with induction using propofol compared with DEX. Greater consideration should be given for use of DEX induction for patients with T21 undergoing sedated radiologic procedures.

articles.title: Follow-up of human papillomavirus positive patients after self-collection in the emergency department.
articles.journal_full: The American journal of emergency medicine

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Emergency department (ED) patients often lack sufficient primary care access and are disproportionately under-screened for cervical cancer compared with the general population. The recent FDA approval of self-collection for HPV testing at healthcare sites may facilitate cervical cancer screening for some patients. Thus, we investigated the proposition that the ED presents an opportunity to engage otherwise hard-to-reach individuals with cervical cancer screening via in-ED self-collection for HPV testing. While HPV negative individuals do not require further screening, HPV positive individuals require additional steps in the outpatient setting to complete screening.

abstract.label: OBJECTIVE
abstract.text: After recent completion of a feasibility study of HPV self-collection among eligible ED patients in which more than 80% of participants agreed to self-collect and approximately 75% successfully completed self-collection in the ED, we followed the individuals who tested positive for HPV to assess their rate of follow-up for outpatient completion of screening.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: We conducted follow-up at 150 days via electronic health record review and telephone survey to determine the follow-up rate for individuals who tested positive for HPV after in-ED self-collection.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Among the individuals who successfully completed self-collection for HPV in the parent study, 24 (15.9%) tested positive for HPV. At 150 days, 7 (29.2%) out of 24 had completed screening (1 additional participant had scheduled upcoming screening). Individuals with higher triage acuity were less likely to follow up for additional screening.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: Additional supports are required to maximize follow-up for completion of screening among those who test positive after in-ED self-collection for HPV testing.

articles.title: Public awareness and self-reported first-aid preparedness for cervical spine injury among adults in Northern Saudi Arabia: A cross-sectional study.

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Cervical spine injuries can result in substantial morbidity and mortality, particularly when early management is inappropriate. Public knowledge of safe first-aid measures may help reduce preventable secondary injury. This study assessed awareness of cervical spine injury and appropriate first-aid responses among adults living in the Northern Border Region of Saudi Arabia.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: This descriptive cross-sectional study was conducted from January to July 2026 among adults aged 18 years and older residing in the Northern Border Region, Saudi Arabia. Data were collected through an online self-administered questionnaire assessing participants' knowledge of cervical spine injury, appropriate first-aid responses, and preparedness. Descriptive statistics were used to summarize the data. Associations between categorical variables were assessed using Pearson's chi-square test, and the correlation between awareness and practice/preparedness scores was evaluated using Pearson's correlation coefficient.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: A total of 605 participants were included. Overall, 62.8% demonstrated good awareness of cervical spine injury and appropriate first-aid responses, whereas 37.2% had poor awareness. The mean awareness score was 8.88 ± 3.91. Good practice/preparedness regarding appropriate first-aid responses was reported by 86.8% of participants, while 13.2% had poor practice/preparedness. The mean practice/preparedness score was 3.52 ± 0.91 out of 4. Awareness scores showed a moderate positive correlation with practice/preparedness scores (r = 0.477, p < 0.001).

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: Although awareness and preparedness were generally favorable, important knowledge gaps remained. Community-based first-aid education should emphasize minimizing unnecessary movement, maintaining cervical spine stabilization when injury is suspected, and promptly activating emergency medical services.

articles.title: Shift change: 12- versus 24-hour work period models in acute care surgery.
Nursing led protocols in trauma: a point-counterpoint analysis.

abstract.text: This narrative point-counterpoint analysis examines the benefits, risks, and implementation requirements of nursing-led medication administration protocols in trauma and emergency care. It draws on the debate at the 2026 Maryland Committee on Trauma Point/Counterpoint XLIII Conference in Baltimore and selected published literature to develop practical recommendations for clinical use and evaluation. The conference proposition that these protocols save lives is examined critically; this article does not report an original outcomes study. Reported benefits include earlier medication administration, improved symptom management, and more consistent delivery of indicated treatment. One randomized emergency department evaluation reported a 186-min reduction in median time to acetaminophen, and a retrospective intracerebral hemorrhage cohort associated nursing-led protocol changes with faster blood pressure control. These findings support improvements in care processes but do not establish a general survival benefit in trauma. Risks include inappropriate patient selection, medication errors, delayed escalation, and excessive protocol complexity. Safe implementation requires multidisciplinary agreement on scope, clear eligibility and exclusion criteria, accessible escalation pathways, and education that accounts for staff turnover and fatigue. Protocols should be integrated into trauma and emergency performance improvement processes to monitor adherence, treatment timeliness, adverse events, and patient outcomes, with feedback and reassessment after corrective action. Nursing-led medication protocols can improve timely care when supported by these safeguards; their effectiveness and sustainability require ongoing evaluation in the populations and settings where they are used.

articles.title: Should MAP augmentation remain the standard therapy after traumatic spinal cord injury?

abstract.text: Traumatic spinal cord injury (SCI) remains one of the most devastating injuries in trauma care. For nearly three decades, maintenance of elevated mean arterial pressure (MAP) has been advocated to mitigate secondary ischemic injury after SCI and help preserve or improve neurologic outcomes. Although current guidelines continue to recommend augmentation of MAP and strict avoidance of hypotension, the supporting evidence remains predominantly observational. At the 41st Annual Point/counterpoint Acute Care Surgery Conference, experts debated whether MAP augmentation remains necessary after SCI. This review summarizes the physiologic rationale, supporting and opposing clinical evidence, emerging concepts in spinal cord perfusion pressure, and future directions in hemodynamic management. Level of evidence: III.

articles.title: Psychometric Evaluation of the Persian Version of the Disaster Resilience Measurement Scale for Healthcare Rescuers (DRMS-HR): A Cross-Sectional Validation Study.

abstract.label: BACKGROUND AND AIMS
abstract.text: The resilience of responders is crucial for effective performance under pressure. The Disaster Resilience Measurement Scale for Healthcare Rescuers (DRMS-HR) was developed specifically for pre-hospital emergency staff. This study aims to assess the DRMS-HR in Iran.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: This cross-sectional validation study involved the translation and cultural adaptation of the DRMS-HR using the forward-backward method. Psychometric properties were assessed in a sample of 303 pre-hospital emergency personnel. Validity was evaluated through face validity (via cognitive interviews and impact scores), content validity (using the Content Validity Ratio and Content Validity Index with 10 experts), and construct validity via Confirmatory Factor Analysis. Reliability was examined through internal consistency (Cronbach's alpha) and test-retest reliability using the Intraclass Correlation Coefficient (ICC) with a subsample of 30 emergency health workers.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Face validity of the translated version of the questionnaire was confirmed. Content Validity indices composed of the CVR and CVI fell within acceptable ranges. Four items were excluded from the scale due to their standardized factor loading values falling below the threshold of 0.3. Reliability assessments indicated strong internal consistency for the instrument, with Cronbach's alpha values of 0.864. The ICC for the tool was at 0.921, demonstrating satisfactory reproducibility of the instrument.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: The DRMS-HR is a reliable and valid scale for assessing the resilience among pre-hospital emergency staff.

articles.title: Aggregating Pre-Hospital and In-Hospital Databases of Trauma Patients: A Descriptive Cross-Sectional Study.

abstract.label: BACKGROUND AND AIMS
abstract.text: Trauma-related deaths are a major public health issue, with different organizations playing a role in decreasing these deaths, including pre-hospital and in-hospital care. Patient data in these organizations are gathered in siloed datasets, which necessitates data integration of these datasets to help decision-makers better understand factors related to trauma mortality.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: This descriptive cross-sectional study included all trauma patients treated at Rajaei Hospital from 1 March to 30 October 2024. Data from the Emergency Center in Shiraz database and Shiraz Care Monitoring Center database were obtained, and a heuristic record-linkage algorithm was used to integrate these data using patient names, age, sex, and time of arrival. Demographic characteristics, injury mechanisms, transport, prehospital times, and outcomes were extracted from the linked dataset. Manual review included 1000 randomly selected hospital records. Descriptive summaries and exploratory two-sided comparisons of mortality proportions were reported.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Linkage performance showed precision of 97.11% (95% CI, 94.89%-98.38%), recall of 87.44% (83.94%-90.27%), and an F1-score of 92.02% (90.07%-93.97%). The hospital cohort included 29,891 trauma patients; 281/29,891 died. A total of 131 patients died within 24 h, including 114 patients at triage level 1. Approximately 88% of deaths were due to blunt trauma. Higher mortality proportions were observed in older age groups.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: The presented heuristic record-linkage algorithm is a pragmatic approach to integrating data from two complex datasets, and the integrated dataset could be used in future studies to examine relationships between mortality and patient characteristics.

articles.title: Introducing the Open Educational Resource PAVIN: a blended-learning, interprofessional multiplayer virtual reality training in paediatric emergencies.

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: The inherent dynamics of paediatric emergencies create substantial challenges for interprofessional teams and limit the availability of an optimal learning environment for developing emergency‑care competencies. Consequently, there is an increasing demand for educational approaches that replicate the dynamics of paediatric emergencies while offering a safe learning environment. Virtual reality (VR) scenarios deliver realistic, repeatable training experiences that allow novice interprofessional teams to acquire their first exposure in challenging situations. To encounter the demand paediatric-emergency trainings, we aimed to implement a blended-learning course that couples e-learning modules with VR scenarios and incorporates objective feedback systems.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: We developed the Paediatric virtual reality emergency training (PAVIN), an interprofessional blended-learning course that integrates three complementary components: (1) preparatory e‑learning modules, (2) on-site sessions and (3) multiplayer VR scenarios. The case‑based e‑learning modules supply the theoretical basic medical knowledge and introduce essential non‑technical skills in communication and interprofessional collaboration. Interprofessional tandems - comprising medical, nursing and midwifery students and nursing apprentices - subsequently train in multiplayer VR simulations, offering a safe, reproducible learning environment.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: The pilot phase demonstrated that PAVIN could be implemented successfully. Of the ten participants, nine (90% response rate) completed the evaluation questionnaire and awarded the course an overall "very good" rating. They gave positive scores across several self-reported domains: they judged the course highly relevant to their future work, reported heightened interest in interprofessional learning and found the blended-learning framework appropriate. Moreover, participants reported that the immersive VR scenarios helped them internalise paediatric-emergency procedures and that communication and collaboration with their tandem partner improved. We integrated multiple feedback mechanisms throughout the course, encompassing both the e-learning modules and the multiplayer VR scenarios, which participants found useful. They are supplemented with team-performance instruments, such as the virtual Team Performance Observation Tool (vTPOT) and pre- and post-intervention self-assessments.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: PAVIN is a blended-learning course that offers a safe environment for participants to gain experience in paediatric-emergency care and communication while training in interprofessional teams. Multiple feedback systems are embedded to enable data-driven debriefings. Available as an Open Educational Resource (OER), PAVIN may represent a promising approach for interprofessional medical education, could help meet the ongoing demand for paediatric-emergency training and might has the potential to support medical education in patient safety.

articles.title: Point-of-care ultrasound of the upper airway for direct confirmation of correct endotracheal tube placement in paediatric patients: analysis of 110 cases.

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Point-of-care ultrasound of the upper airway can rapidly confirm the anatomical position of the endotracheal tube without the need for preliminary ventilation. However, evidence on specific sonographic signs in children remains limited.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: This prospective, single-centre, observational study included children undergoing elective ENT surgery under general anesthesia. The study assessed four predefined ultrasound signs of the upper airway: the snowstorm sign, the bullet sign, the tracheal dilatation sign, and the absence of the double-track sign. Bilateral lung sliding was also evaluated. Correct intubation was defined as quantitative capnography combined with bilateral chest auscultation. The sensitivity, positive and negative predictive values, and 95% confidence intervals were estimated for the individual signs, combinations of signs, and a cumulative ultrasound score.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: A total of 104 children were included in the study, of whom 103 had correct tracheal intubation. The sensitivity was found to be 81.6% for the snowstorm sign, 75.7% for the tracheal dilatation sign, 53.4% for the bullet sign and 100% for both the absence of the double-track sign and bilateral lung sliding. At least one positive dynamic sign showed 85.4% sensitivity, while at least one positive static sign or a cumulative score of at least one both achieved 100% sensitivity. The positive predictive values were consistently high, reflecting the absence of false positives in a cohort with almost exclusively successful intubations.

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: Upper-airway point-of-care ultrasound appears feasible as an adjunct for confirming paediatric orotracheal intubation. Static signs were identified more consistently than some dynamic signs. Further studies including sufficient esophageal or misplaced intubations are needed to establish specificity and overall diagnostic accuracy.

articles.title: Exposure technology and tissue protection in anterior and anterolateral thoracic/thoracolumbar fracture surgery: An international surgeon survey of retractor performance, mitigation strategies, and design priorities.

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Anterior and anterolateral thoracic/thoracolumbar fracture surgery can provide direct vertebral-body and ventral canal access but requires controlled exposure through deep, anatomy-constrained corridors. We evaluated surgeon-reported retractor performance, tissue-protection behaviors, and device-design priorities.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: An international web-based survey was completed by 82 surgeons from 22 countries. Detailed analyses were restricted to 39 surgeons who reported personal anterior/anterolateral T4-L2 fracture surgery within 5 years. Likert items, multi-select mitigation strategies, and 26 free-text design responses were summarized descriptively; Rasch hierarchy, specialty differential item functioning (DIF), and MADQ3 residual correlations were exploratory response-structure analyses.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Standard rib spreaders, table-mounted ring retractors, and expandable lateral retractors were each used by 17/39 surgeons (43.6%). Prominent signals were large body habitus increasing difficulty and pressure (28/33, 84.8%), adjunct visualization (28/35, 80.0%), T11-L2 working distance (27/34, 79.4%), stability/minimal creep (26/37, 70.3%), and blade geometry (21/31, 67.7%). Common protective strategies were avoiding the inferior-rib neurovascular bundle (23/39, 59.0%), periodic partial release (20/39, 51.3%), and limiting blade opening according to imaging or chest-wall size (15/39, 38.5%). Overall soft-tissue risk (7/36, 19.4%) and reported complication frequency (1/33, 3.0%) had lower upper-category endorsement. Design responses prioritized blade geometry/pressure distribution (13/26, 50.0%), integrated illumination (12/26, 46.2%), and imaging/optical integration (11/26, 42.3%). No DIF signal survived false-discovery-rate correction.

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: Surgeons conceptualized safe exposure as a coupled mechanical, visual, and tissue-loading problem. Future retractor systems should be evaluated at depth for stability, pressure distribution, blade geometry, illumination, imaging compatibility, and workflow using objective bench and cadaveric metrics.

articles.title: Ultrasound-Guided Suprascapular Nerve Block Versus Intravenous Fentanyl for Analgesia in Patients Presenting to the Emergency Department With Traumatic Scapular Fractures.

abstract.label: STUDY OBJECTIVE
abstract.text: To compare the analgesic efficacy and safety of ultrasound-guided suprascapular nerve block with intravenous fentanyl in patients with traumatic scapular fractures.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: We conducted an open-label randomized controlled pilot trial in the emergency department (ED) of a Level I trauma center in North India. Adults with traumatic scapular fractures and Defense and Veterans Pain Rating Scale scores of 7 and higher, were randomly assigned to ultrasound-guided suprascapular nerve block or intravenous fentanyl (1 μg/kg). Pain scores were assessed at baseline and 30, 60, 120, 240, and 360 minutes. Secondary outcomes included rescue analgesia and adverse events.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Sixty patients were randomly assigned to the 2 groups. Median baseline pain score was 10 in both groups. Pain scores were consistently lower with suprascapular nerve block, with median scores of 3 (interquartile [IQR] 2 to 5) versus 7 (IQR 6 to 8) at 30 minutes. Between-group differences were 4 (95% confidence interval [CI], 3 to 4) at 30 and 60 minutes, 2 (95% CI, 2 to 2) at 120 and 240 minutes, and 1 (95% CI, 1 to 2) at 360 minutes. Rescue analgesia was less frequent with suprascapular nerve block (13% versus 79%; risk difference, -66% [95% CI, 47.5 to 85.2]). Drowsiness was more common with fentanyl (12 versus 2 participants); hypotension occurred in 1 fentanyl recipient and paresthesia in 1 suprascapular nerve block recipient.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: In this pilot randomized trial, ultrasound-guided suprascapular nerve block provided greater and sustained pain relief, reduced rescue analgesia, and fewer systemic adverse effects than intravenous fentanyl in adults with traumatic scapular fractures. Larger multicenter trials are needed to confirm these findings and evaluate cumulative opioid use and longer-term outcomes.

articles.title: Most National Football League Players Return to Play After Achilles Tendon Repair, Yet Only One-Half Regain Preinjury Performance With Persistent Pass-Rush Decline at Year 2.

abstract.label: PURPOSE
abstract.text: To evaluate National Football League (NFL) player performance using advanced statistics after Achilles tendon (AT) repair.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: NFL players who underwent AT repair between 2017 and 2023 were identified from a publicly available injury database. Demographic and performance data were collected preinjury and up to 2 seasons postinjury, with a minimum follow-up of 1 regular-season game required to assess return to play (RTP). RTP was defined as being active for a regular-season game and return to performance as achieving ≥90% of preinjury performance. Performance was assessed using Sports Information Solutions' points above replacement (PAR). Factors associated with RTP and return to performance were analyzed using binary logistic regression, with pre- and postinjury performance compared using paired t tests or Wilcoxon signed-rank tests, as appropriate.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Seventy-seven NFL players with AT repairs were identified. Ten were excluded for no prior regular-season play, leaving 67 included. Overall, 77.6% (n = 52) returned to play. Increasing age reduced the odds of RTP (odds ratio 0.75, 95% confidence interval [0.60-0.95], P = .02). Index games preinjury increased the odds of RTP (odds ratio 1.12, 95% confidence interval [1.01-1.24], P = .04). Body mass index, position, index games played, and index PAR were not significant. Among returnees, 50% (n = 26) achieved at least 90% of preinjury performance. Higher index PAR predicted lower odds of meeting this threshold (odds ratio 0.77, 95% confidence interval [0.66-0.90], P = .00). Pass-rush PAR declined at year 2 after injury from 1.17 (±5.19) preinjury to -0.66 (±2.15), P = .02.

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: In this study using publicly available data, 77.6% of NFL players returned to play after AT repair; however, only one-half of these players regained ≥90% of their preinjury performance. Older age reduced the likelihood of RTP, whereas more preinjury games started increased it. Higher preinjury PAR reduced the likelihood of performance recovery. Pass-rush performance declined by the second postinjury season.

abstract.label: LEVEL OF EVIDENCE
abstract.text: Level IV, retrospective therapeutic case series.

articles.title: MPLA preconditioning protects against lethal radiation-combined burn injury with attenuation of KC/CXCL1-associated vascular leakage in mice.

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Radiation-combined burn injury (RCB), defined as concurrent irradiation and burn injury, is expected to be common in radiological or nuclear mass-casualty events and can be highly lethal. The mechanisms underlying the irradiation-burn interaction remain poorly understood, particularly whether it amplifies capillary leak and inflammatory mediator responses to drive early lethality. We examined whether repeated low-dose monophosphoryl lipid A (MPLA) preconditioning modulates this response and whether KC/CXCL1 contributes to vascular leakage.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: Male C57BL/6J mice underwent 6 Gy whole-body irradiation followed 1 h later by a 20% total body surface area full-thickness burn. MPLA (10 µg/mouse) or vehicle was administered intraperitoneally on days -4 and -3. We assessed 30-day survival, hemoconcentration, intravascular FITC-albumin retention, intestinal barrier endpoints, and cytokine/chemokine responses. A separate exploratory experiment evaluated pre-irradiation anti-KC/CXCL1 antibody treatment.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Neither injury alone was lethal, whereas vehicle-treated RCB mice had 90% mortality (9 of 10 mice). Seven of these deaths occurred at 24-48 h after RCB. MPLA preconditioning increased 30-day survival from 10% to 80% (p = 0.0003) and eliminated deaths within 48 h. RCB induced hemoconcentration and tended to reduce FITC-albumin retention. Compared with vehicle-treated RCB mice, MPLA-preconditioned RCB mice had less hemoconcentration, significantly higher FITC-albumin retention, and lower mesenteric lymph node bacterial burden. MPLA preconditioning suppressed KC/CXCL1, which showed the largest absolute increase among measured cytokines/chemokines at 6 h. Anti-KC/CXCL1 antibody treatment significantly increased FITC-albumin retention at 6 h (p = 0.038).

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: MPLA preconditioning improved survival after RCB. It may attenuate early inflammatory and vascular abnormalities. Exploratory antibody-treatment findings suggest a possible contribution of KC/CXCL1 to early vascular albumin leakage, warranting further validation.

articles.title: Geographic accessibility and drowning outcomes within a universal healthcare system: a nationwide population-based study.

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: The impact of structural healthcare determinants on drowning survival within universal health coverage (UHC) systems remains unclear. This study evaluated whether increased geographic distance to emergency responsibility hospitals (ERHs) is associated with worse drowning outcomes in Taiwan.

abstract.label: MATERIALS AND METHODS
abstract.text: This nationwide retrospective cohort study analyzed 1,361 acute drowning patients transported to emergency departments (2014-2019) from the Taiwan National Health Insurance Research Database. Outcomes were categorized by 90-day severity: mild, severe (requiring intubation, resuscitation, or presenting in a coma), or fatal. Straight-line Euclidean distance from the treating hospital's district centroid (a proxy for incident location) to the nearest ERH quantified geographic proximity. A multivariable proportional odds model evaluated the association between distance and outcome severity, adjusting for demographic and clinical covariates.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Overall, 207 patients had severe outcomes (15.2%) and 301 were fatal (22.1%). Each additional kilometer to the nearest ERH was significantly associated with higher odds of a worse outcome (adjusted odds ratio [aOR] 1.11 per km; 95% CI 1.02-1.21; p = 0.0116). The distance-by-ERH-tier interaction was non-significant (p = 0.309), indicating distance effects persist regardless of institutional capability. Regionally, mean distance correlated positively with mean outcome severity (R2 = 18.33%).

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: Under UHC, geographic proximity to emergency care is a primary structural determinant of drowning survival; greater distance independently predicts worse outcomes. While advanced ERHs confer survival benefits, these are constrained by transport distances across all tiers, making rapid access and early stabilization paramount.

articles.title: [Emergency critical care in the emergency department].

abstract.text: Emergency critical care (ECC) provides early, ongoing critical care outside the intensive care unit (ICU). This narrative review describes organizational models and evidence in emergency medicine. Predominantly retrospective, single-center studies indicate that critical care is initiated earlier and that there are fewer subsequent inpatient ICU admissions. Neither a consistent mortality benefit nor the superiority of any model has been established. ECC supports early care, coordination of complex care pathways, and needs-based resource allocation, guided by the principle: the right patient in the right care setting.

articles.title: Impact of heat alerts on mortality and emergency ambulance dispatches in Japan.

abstract.text: Heat-health warning systems are important measures used worldwide to mitigate heat-related illness, but evidence on their effectiveness remains inconsistent. Japan has seen a rise in heatstroke cases in recent years, prompting the implementation of a heat alert system to prevent health risks. This study evaluates the impact of Japan's heat alert system on mortality and emergency ambulance dispatches (EADs). We collected daily time-series data on mortality, EADs, and Wet Bulb Globe Temperature (WBGT) across Japan's 47 prefectures for June-September 2020 and May-September 2021-2023; mortality data were available only through 2022. For both mortality and EADs, data were collected for all-cause, circulatory, respiratory, and genitourinary outcomes. Additionally, EADs were collected for heatstroke. Heat alert days were matched with non-alert days with similar WBGT levels. A conditional Poisson regression model was used to evaluate the association between heat alerts and health outcomes. Of 2,715 heat alert days between 2020 and 2023, 1,310 had matched non-alert counterparts, resulting in 2,620 observation days. EADs increased on heat alert days: all-cause by 3.11% (95% confidence interval (CI): 1.74%, 4.50%), genitourinary by 5.82% (95% CI: 0.07%, 11.9%), and heatstroke by 31.1% (95% CI: 21.2%, 41.8%) compared to matched non-alert days. No significant associations were observed for mortality or other EAD outcomes. These patterns may be associated with heightened public awareness, diagnostic shifts, or behavioral responses. Further research should explore public engagement with alerts and behavioral changes in response to heat alerts.

articles.title: Evaluation of pediatric patients diagnosed with food protein-induced enterocolitis syndrome.

abstract.label: UNLABELLED
abstract.text: Food Protein-Induced Enterocolitis Syndrome (FPIES) is a non-IgE-mediated food allergy typically presenting in infancy with heterogeneous clinical manifestations. The absence of specific biomarkers complicates diagnosis and management. This study aimed to evaluate demographic characteristics, trigger food distribution, clinical phenotypes, and tolerance development in pediatric patients diagnosed with FPIES. This cross-sectional study included pediatric patients diagnosed with FPIES and followed at Ankara Etlik City Hospital between October 2022 and December 2025. Patients were re-evaluated for demographic data, trigger foods, phenotypic features, oral food challenge (OFC) outcomes, and tolerance development. A total of 63 patients were included (63.5% male), with a median age of 26 months (IQR 16-37). A total of 134 reactions were documented, with a median age at first reaction of 7 months (IQR 6-8). During first acute episodes, 19 patients required emergency care; three were hospitalized, and two required intensive care unit admission. Egg yolk was the most common trigger (51.5%), followed by cow's milk (21.2%), fish (18.1%), egg white (6%), and red meat (3%). Multiple trigger foods were identified in three patients. Phenotypic analysis revealed atypical FPIES in 10 patients and chronic FPIES in one patient. A total of 34 OFCs were performed for diagnostic confirmation and tolerance assessment. Reactions occurred in 11 tests, and eight required medical treatment. During follow-up, tolerance developed in 47.6% (n = 30) of patients, with a median tolerance age of 18 months (IQR 14-26). Tolerance was confirmed by OFC in 18 patients and by successful home reintroduction in 12.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: In this single-center cohort, egg yolk was the predominant trigger food. Nearly half of the patients achieved early tolerance. Given the heterogeneous phenotypic spectrum of FPIES, increased clinical awareness and standardized management approaches are essential for optimal follow-up and prognosis assessment.

abstract.label: WHAT IS KNOWN
abstract.text: • FPIES shows geographic variation in trigger foods and clinical presentation, and tolerance acquisition may differ according to the culprit food.

abstract.label: WHAT IS NEW
abstract.text: • Egg yolk was the predominant trigger in this cohort, while fish-induced FPIES showed significantly later tolerance acquisition, supporting food-specific timing of follow-up and re-evaluation.

articles.title: Detecting deterioration of children in emergency departments requires more than a score alone.
Transorbital retained foreign body of the infratemporal fossa presenting as a parotid abscess: an unlikely route of spread.
Validation of Primary and Hospital Care Resource Use and Cost Estimates in OMOP-mapped vs Source Healthcare Administrative Datasets.
articles.journal_full: Value in health : the journal of the International Society for Pharmacoeconomics and Outcomes Research

abstract.label: OBJECTIVES
abstract.text: To assess whether estimates of primary and hospital care resource use and costs from Observational Medical Outcomes Partnership (OMOP) Common Data Model (CDM) mapped data are consistent with source healthcare administrative datasets and to discuss implications for OMOP-based health economic analyses.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: We conducted a retrospective cohort study (2010-2018) of women aged >50 years with a fragility fracture. Analyses were performed in parallel using source Clinical Practice Research Datalink Aurum linked to Hospital Episode Statistics data and two OMOP-based strategies: OMOP-standard (standardised concepts only) and OMOP-source (also including source variables). Primary and hospital care utilisation and costs were estimated over two years. Mean differences were summarised with bootstrapped 95% confidence intervals.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Cohorts were comparable (23,106 source; 22,900 OMOP), with similar characteristics and follow-up. Resource utilisation was consistent across databases (<1% difference). Total cost differences were 2.2% (OMOP-standard) and 1.7% (OMOP-source, not statistically significant). Primary care, inpatient and outpatient cost differences were ≤3% among costed records. Emergency care costs were ∼21% lower in both OMOP strategies, reflecting a different costing method rather than mapping fidelity (0.1% when the same method was applied to source data). Discrepancies were mainly due to costing assumptions, and less so to incomplete vocabularies and structural constraints.

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: OMOP-mapped data produced resource use estimates highly consistent and aggregate cost estimates concordant with source data. Remaining cost discrepancies were concentrated in specific settings and reduced when source variables were used. Refining mapping and costing approaches will improve accuracy and support federated economic research using OMOP-CDM.

articles.title: IDEntifying pAtients with suspicion of infection in the ED who have Low disease severity using midregional proadrenomedullin (MR-proADM) - A pragmatic pivotal randomised controlled trial.
articles.journal_full: Clinical microbiology and infection : the official publication of the European Society of Clinical Microbiology and Infectious Diseases

abstract.label: OBJECTIVES
abstract.text: Concentrations of blood biomarker midregional-proadrenomedullin (MR-proADM) can reflect the early microvascular changes and organ dysfunction, which drive the pathophysiology of sepsis. Observational studies and a single-country randomised trial suggested MR-proADM could assist emergency department (ED) clinicians with regards to safer discharges or admission avoidance. The objective of this trial is to evaluate the efficacy/safety of incorporating MR-proADM, into clinical decision-making for hospitalisation or discharge in patients presenting with clinical suspicion of infection to EDs in different countries.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: An open-label randomised-controlled, interventional trial, conducted across nine European EDs. Patients with suspicion of infection and unclear decision of hospitlisataion in the EDs were randomised 1:1 to either MR-proADM-guided algorithm for admission or discharge from ED or to the standard care (SC) arms. The primary efficacy endpoint was the proportion of patients admitted to hospital targeting a reduction in hospitalisation by the intervention compared to SC. The primary safety objective was to show non-inferiority (against 14% margin) in 5-day all-cause ED re-presentation.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: In low severity illness setting, among 460 patients enrolled a similar hospitalisation rate was seen between the MR-proADM (80/230=34.8%) and the SC (78/230=33.9%) arms in the intention to treat (ITT) population, i.e. a rate difference of 0.9% with 95% CI from -7.8% to 9.5% (p=0.922). In the per-protocol (PP) population, there were fewer admissions (43/168=25.6% when MR-proADM guided vs. 77/221=34.8% in SC), but statistically not significant. Re-presentation within 5-days demonstrated non-inferiority for the MR-proADM-guided arm versus the SC in the PP population with a rate reduction estimated at -2.5% (95% CI [-9.5%, 4.6%], p=0.607).

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: In this study, the addition of MR-proADM was not associated with statistically different hospitalisation rate. [trial registration: ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT05108883)] Date: November 3rd, 2021.

articles.title: Trends in United States Pediatric In-Hospital Cardiac Arrest Incidence and Mortality in a Nationally Representative Sample, 2009-2022.

abstract.label: AIM
abstract.text: National estimates of pediatric in-hospital cardiac arrest (IHCA) incidence in the United States rely on a voluntary registry that may underrepresent smaller and critical access hospitals. Administrative datasets offer a nationally representative alternative. We estimated nationally representative pediatric IHCA incidence and mortality trends from 2009 through 2022.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: Serial cross-sectional analysis of five triennial editions of the Kids' Inpatient Database (2009-2022), identifying IHCA in children <18 years by ICD-9 (99.60, 99.63) and ICD-10 (5A12012) cardiopulmonary resuscitation procedure codes. Two hospitals with implausible CPR rates were excluded. Survey-weighted incidence per 1,000 hospitalizations and in-hospital mortality among resuscitated children were estimated overall and by neonatal status, complex chronic condition (CCC) status, ZIP-code income quartile, and US Census region. Trends were tested with survey-weighted quasi-Poisson regression across the full period and, as exploratory analyses, within the ICD-10 era (2016-2022).

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Observed IHCA incidence was 1.11/1,000 in 2009 and 1.22/1,000 in 2012, decreased to 1.11/1,000 at the ICD-10 transition and increased to 1.35/1,000 by 2022. IHCA incidence in children hospitalized with a CCC rose from 3.26 to 6.60/1,000 (6.2%/year, p<0.001), while incidence without CCC remained low. Incidence varied by socioeconomic status (lowest vs highest income quartile 1.78 vs 1.04/1,000 in 2022). In-hospital mortality ranged from 34.1% (2012) to 40.4% (2019), whereas IHCA deaths per 1,000 hospitalizations increased 1.7%/year (p<0.001), concentrated among children with a CCC.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: The incidence of pediatric IHCA increased among hospitalizations involving children with CCC and was higher among children who live in lower income areas. In-hospital mortality after CPR was largely stable, whereas arrest-related deaths per 1,000 hospitalizations increased among children with CCC. A single hospital's coding practices can materially distort national administrative estimates. What is already known Pediatric in-hospital cardiac arrest affects approximately 15,200 children annually in the United States, with this national estimate derived primarily from a voluntary registry that may underrepresent smaller and critical access hospitals. Administrative databases offer nationally representative coverage but rely on procedure codes that are susceptible to misclassification. What this study adds In this nationally representative administrative database sample spanning 2009-2022, this study demonstrated that: 1) the incidence of IHCA among children with complex chronic conditions (CCC) rose steadily and accounted for the substantial majority of events, 2) the overall IHCA incidence was higher among children who live in lower income areas with the gradient worsening over the period evaluated, and 3) in-hospital mortality after CPR increased only slightly (34-40%), whereas arrest-related deaths per 1,000 hospitalizations increased more, driven mainly by rising incidence among children with CCC, and 4) CPR coding at a single hospital can substantially distort national administrative estimates.

articles.title: Imaging After Retinal Artery Occlusion Versus Transient Ischemic Attack.

abstract.text: Among 3695 matched pairs with same-date emergency department contact, retinal artery occlusion was associated with lower brain imaging use (77.3% versus 91.7%) and slightly higher cervical imaging use (81.7% versus 79.2%) than transient ischemic attack.

articles.title: The Effects of Non-Psoriatic Dermatitis on Total Hip Arthroplasty Outcomes: A Propensity-Matched Analysis with Longitudinal Follow-Up.

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: While psoriasis has been associated with increased complications following total hip arthroplasty (THA), the effects of non-psoriatic dermatitis (NPD) on THA outcomes remain unclear. Therefore, this study evaluated the association between NPD and postoperative outcomes following primary THA with additional stratification by dermatitis-related medication use.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: In a large national database, patients aged ≥ 18 years undergoing primary THA anytime between 2003 and 2020 were identified. Patients who had NPD were compared with a control cohort of patients who did not have NPD. Additional pairwise comparisons evaluated the effect of dermatitis-related medication use. After multiple demographics and comorbidities were propensity-matched using a 1:1 ratio, postoperative medical outcomes and surgical complications were examined with follow-up at 90 days, one year, and two years.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: At 90 days, NPD was associated with a higher rate of emergency department admission and a lower rate of periprosthetic dislocation or instability (P ≤ 0.048). There were no other significant associations observed at one or two years. Compared to patients who do not have NPD, patients who have NPD with concurrent medication use had higher rates of inpatient readmission, emergency department admission, deep vein thrombosis, falls, and periprosthetic fracture at 90 days (P ≤ 0.027), and periprosthetic fracture remained elevated at one and two years (P ≤ 0.012). Patients who have NPD without medication use showed no significant differences for all measured outcomes across every timepoint.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: Although some 90-day outcomes were significant, NPD was not independently associated with one- and two-year complications following THA. Patients receiving medications for NPD treatment may represent a high-risk subgroup with increased healthcare utilization, thromboembolic events, falls, and periprosthetic fracture. Among THA candidates who have NPD, the effects of pharmaceutical management may be considered, especially for thromboembolic risk, fall prevention, and bone health optimization.

articles.title: Capillary refill time at the admission of trauma patients: A prospective, observational study.

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: The early identification of tissue perfusion is a significant challenge in the management of severe trauma cases. Capillary refill time (CRT) is a simple clinical marker of peripheral perfusion. The objective of this study was to ascertain the correlation between CRT and serum lactate levels in patients with severe trauma.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: A prospective, single-center observational study was conducted in a 20-bed intensive care unit (ICU) of a level 1 trauma center between April 2025 and January 2026. Adult patients who were directly admitted to the ICU from the scene of the accident for severe trauma, as defined by an injury severity score above 15, were included in the study. The CRT and serum lactate were measured on admission to the ICU. The primary endpoint was the association between admission serum lactate and admission CRT ≥ 3 s (abnormal CRT). Secondary analyses included the correlation between CRT and serum lactate at admission and the association between CRT and duration of vasopressor exposure during the first 3 days. Multivariate linear regression was performed on logarithmically transformed serum lactate, adjusted for age, core body temperature, prehospital weight-adjusted fluid administration, prehospital use of norepinephrine and prehospital timing.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Of 627 patients screened, 196 were included in the analysis. The admission CRT was 2.4 [1.7-3.1] s with serum lactate level at 2.1 [1.3-3.4] mmol/L.
